doc.title: Ed Soph interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, February 9, 2024

title: Getting students to listen to the past: Baby Dodds
summary: Soph says students resist older recordings; he recalls wearing out his father's LPs and his first hero Baby Dodds.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Yeah I was going to ask right at the beginning of this wonderful description you said, “aural.” I’m assuming you’re going A-U-R-A-L. Correct?
Yeah. Because if there’s a lot like oral history and so forth.

Oh yeah. That’s important too, that that’s the other thing. I don’t make any value judgments because invariably they’re wrong in some form or another. But what I will say is that the hardest thing to do with most students is to get them to listen to the past. Because there’s such great peer pressure to be hip and current. And I talk to my students, I say, “When I was a kid and my father would bring home at first 78s but later on 33-1/3 LPs” and I said, “I would play those damn things until I, without knowing, I was singing horn solos. You know? I quit listening to the drums, quit listening to my instrument, and started listening to the band.” And I said, “That was so valuable.” And I said, “Even more so, my first drum hero was Baby Dodds.” And they go, “Who’s Baby Dod —” No they don’t do that, so I say, “Do you know Baby Dodds?” “Oh yeah, yeah, he’s considered the father of jazz drumming.” And then of course that’s my chance. I say, “Okay, play me time the way Baby Dodds did.” Uh oh. I say, “That’s your mistake. You know names but you don’t know the music that goes with the name.”
And that is increasingly, in my experience — where now it’s, “Yes, I’ve seen it on YouTube.” And considering most people’s attention span maybe they watched Baby Dodds for 30 seconds.

That’s what I was getting at when I got a little off track there about listening to a recording. We’d listen — we didn’t have YouTube. And this is not saying oh let’s go back to the good old days, it’s just a matter of we had no choice but to listen to that record over and over and over and over and realizing that every time we listened to it we heard something new. It’s like reading Huckleberry Finn when you’re 12 years old and then reading Huckleberry Finn when you’re 50 years old. A whole different ballgame. Well it’s the same way with this music, whether it’s jazz or classical or anything. Because it’s not just obviously the hands and feet that develop, it’s the ears, which is the bottom line for all of us. So I’ve got to say you don’t need to practice your drums, you need to practice your ears too. And you go back and listen to Baby Dodds and you’ll hear Baby Dodds playing some of the same rhythms that Jack DeJohnette plays or Elvin Jones played. You’ll start to hook into the tradition. It’s all there it’s just voiced differently and moved around in different ways on the kit, but that basic groove is right back there with Baby Dodds. So getting them to go to the past is difficult because their peers are all saying, “Hey man, you’ve got to listen to this latest —” so-and-so. And then the other thing is just lighting, if it’s not already lit try to light their flame of curiosity.
